Nasal cavity tumors are usually diagnosed late, when they already have infiltrated adjacent tissues thus requiring very aggressive treatments with serious side effects. Here we useelectrochemotherapy(ECT), a well demonstrated treatment modality for superficial tumors. MATERIALS AND METHODS:In the case of deep-seated tumors, the main limitation of ECT is reaching the tumor with an appropriate electric field. To overcome this limitation we introduce the single needle electrode (SiNE), a minimally invasive device that can deliver an appropriate electric field with a simple procedure. Twenty-one canine patients with spontaneous tumors were selected, eleven were treated using the SiNE with ECT, and ten with surgery plus adjuvant chemotherapy as a control group.RESULTS:In the SiNE group, 27% achieved a complete response, 64% had a partial response, and 9% had a stable disease. This means that 91% of objective responses were obtained. The mean overall survival was 16.86 months (4-32 months, median 16.5 months), with a survival rate significantly higher (p = 0.0008) when compared with control group. The only side effect observed was the inflammation of the treatednasalpassage, which was controlled with corticosteroid therapy for one week. One year after the treatment, 60% of the canine of the SiNE group vs. 10% of the control group remained alive, and after the 32 months follow-up, the survival rate were 30% and 0%, respectively. CONCLUSIONS: ECT with the SiNE can be safely used in canine to treatnasaltumors with encouraging results. Those clients not electing to participate with this therapy will be followed and data used for comparison. Rechecks may also be done with RDVM but advanced imaging post treatment would be necessary to follow response. While the study is for canine patients, there is no reason not to look at feline and wildlife with the same or similar diagnosis.


The procedure involves a short general anesthesia and is generally an outpatient procedure. Minimal side-effects have been noted and anti-inflammatory pain management may be necessary for a few days post procedure

It is an aggressive tumor with local bone destruction and severe pain where it originates and early metastasis (spread) to other sites within the body. The primary site of metastasis is to the lungs with >90% of dogs having at least microscopic metastasis at the time of diagnosis. Therefore, although surgical removal of the tumor via amputation of the affected limb provides palliation, these patients will eventually die from the development of multiple tumors within the lungs in only a few months. The addition of chemotherapy to address these secondary tumors increases survival over amputation alone and has been the accepted standard of care (SOC) for decades. However, the average survival still does not exceed a year and only a small percentage of dogs survive two years or longer. Thus, more effective treatment protocols are desperately needed. In human oncology, an approach that has been previously investigated is the delivery of low-dose radiation to the lungs (total lung irradiation; TLI) in the hopes of killing the microscopic cancer cells that are present. In these human studies, low-dose TLI, alone or combined with chemotherapy, was found to be safe but clinical benefit varied. Although safety data exists for TLI in healthy and tumor-bearing dogs, its effect on survival in dogs with OSA has been studied on a very limited and non-optimized basis and never in conjunction with SOC: amputation and chemotherapy. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate TLI plus SOC for dogs with OSA in a prospective clinical trial. After undergoing amputation (either here at NC State or at another institution) dogs will be enrolled and starting within 3 days following surgery will begin a protocol of 10 daily fractions of TLI followed by 6 doses of carboplatin chemotherapy (as per our protocol for the adjuvant treatment of canine OSA; may be performed here at NC State \"preferred\" or with another veterinarian if the clients cannot pursue chemotherapy here). Following completion of the carboplatin protocol dogs will then be monitored with serial thoracic radiographs performed every 2 months (our standard practice) to assess for metastatic disease and any potential adverse effects of TLI. Our primary objective is to evaluate the effect of adding TLI to SOC on metastasis-free interval (MFI; the time from amputation to development of the aforementioned lung nodules or spread elsewhere, e.g. bone) and overall survival time (ST; the time from amputation to death or euthanasia). This work aims to evaluate novel combinations of immune therapies in dogs with previously untreated brain tumors to determine the combination that provides the longest remission times with minimal adverse effects. Our ultimate goal is to develop a safe and effective postoperative treatment that avoids the standard therapy with chemotherapy and radiation therapy that can be translated to human GBM patients. Dogs with clinical signs (symptoms) that suggest the presence of a brain mass or tumor will be eligible for participation. Each dog should have a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study of the brain to determine the location, size, and imaging characteristics of the mass. A small sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) may be collected for analysis after the MRI. Dr. Pluhar, the Principal Investigator, will examine the MRI to determine whether the characteristics of the mass are consistent with a diagnosis of glioma that is amenable to surgical removal, which would make your dog eligible to participate in the treatment study. Thorough physical and neurological examinations, blood screening tests, and imaging of the chest and abdomen should be done to make sure that your dog is healthy enough to undergo general anesthesia. If your dog is in adequate physical condition based on these tests, he/she can be enrolled in the study. Inclusion criteria will be: (i) any dog with an intracranial mass and MRI consistent with diagnosis of GBM that is (ii) suitable for surgical resection; (iii) is healthy enough to undergo chemotherapy; and (iv) informed consent provided by the dogs owner. Note: Dogs that do not display a GBM diagnosis upon surgical biopsy will not continue in the trial, but will be treated by standard care. The Exclusion criteria for our trial will be (i) severe neurologic dysfunction, especially changes in level of consciousness that may indicate pending brain herniation; (ii) tumor not amenable to surgical resection; (iii) existence of concomitant disease that would affect the dogs long-term prognosis and preclude completion of chemotherapy or vaccine therapy, and (iv) French bulldogs, which we have found do not respond to vaccine-mediated immunotherapy. Study: All dogs that meet the requirements listed above will have a surgical biopsy to definitively identify the specific tumor type and grade at the time of surgical removal of as much of the tumor as possible. All dogs will be randomly assigned to receive one of the three additional immunotherapies as described above to enhance anti-tumor immunity. The vaccine used for immunotherapy will be created from the dog's own tumor cells grown under special conditions that will improve how they stimulate the dog's immune system. The vaccines should cause the dog's immune system to recognize and kill any tumor cells that were not removed during surgery. The gene therapy has been shown to be effective in killing primary brain tumors in rats and mice and safe in a previous study in dogs that was conducted by the PI. After approaching the dog's brain with the appropriate craniotomy, as much of the tumor mass as possible will be removed. The follow up protocol including timing and exams is as follows: Complete physical and neurological examinations and quality of life assessment at each vaccination starting at suture removal about 10 days after surgery. surgery or radiation therapy. New forms of treatment are needed for both dogs and people with osteosarcoma for this reason. The new drug GEM-IB combines a bone-targeting drug (ibandronate) with a potent cancer drug (gemcitabine) to increase the concentration of cancer drug exactly at the site of the tumor. THIS STUDY IS NOW CLOSED Purpose To establish the feasibility, safety, and tolerability of High Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU) in the treatment of canine soft tissue sarcomas (STS), and to characterize the tumor response and time to progression after HIFU treatment. Background Soft Tissue Sarcomas are a common form of cancer in dogs that can invade tissues vital to normal function. As in humans, complete surgical removal remains the treatment of choice, with aggressive surgery recommended to ensure the best outcome. Surgical removal can sometimes be impossible without leg amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be surgically resectable, but it could still recur at the surgical site or spread in a distant site like lymph node or lung. Radiation therapy is often recommended when surgery cannot completely remove the tumor, to help reduce the risk of local recurrence. Unfortunately, these therapeutic approaches can be unsuccessful and associated with significant discomfort, disfigurement, and financial burden to the owner. Thus, there is a need for novel, less invasive, and more effective therapeutic options. High intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) is a non-invasive, outpatient ablative technique that has the potential to answer these unmet needs. Based on previous studies by our team, we hypothesize that a single HIFU treatment in dogs diagnosed with STS will result in complete tumor ablation, with minimal side effects.

The purpose of this study is to compare post-operative pain management after orthopedic surgery in dogs receiving gabapentin alone, versus a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) medication alone, versus gabapentin and NSAID combined. Gabapentin is commonly prescribed, and while known to be safe, the efficacy of gabapentin for pain control acutely after orthopedic surgery in dogs is not known.


Dogs enrolled in this trial will have a complete physical and orthopedic examination in the normal course of the orthopedic appointment. Further screening will include radiographs of the affected limb and full blood work and urinalysis. Dogs will be randomized into one of 3 study groups (all groups receive pain medication(s)); dogs have a 1/3 chance of being in each of the groups. If on pain medications prior to surgery, a 5 to 30 day \"wash-out\" (depending on the exact medication) (\"wash out\" = no pain medications) will be required prior to surgery. Risks of the surgery include infection, problems related to the implants, and local recurrence. Many factors are contributing to the high rate of complications, and one of them is likely the material used to fabricate the implants. 3D-printing can create personalized implants made of a material that the body can replace with its own bone, namely tricalcium phosphate. Over a period of time, the body can grow new viable bone while removing the tricalcium phosphate, such that the metal plate and screws used with limb sparing will be able to be removed after a period of time, leaving the dog with only its own tissues. We hypothesize that if the implant used to replace the segment of bone with the tumor (i.e. endoprosthesis) was made of a material that the body could replace with its own viable bone, many of the complications would not occur or would be easier to treat. Following entry into the study, dogs will have a CT scan of the affected limb prior to surgery. The images obtained with the CT scan will be used to make the 3D-printed implants that will be used in the limb-sparing surgical procedure. Background Soft tissue sarcomas are a common form of cancer in cats, and are sometimes associated with injections or vaccines. They can invade tissues that are vital to normal function, and complete surgical removal can be impossible without amputation or radiation therapy. In some cases, a tumor may be removable by surgery, but it could still recur at the surgical site or in a distant site like lymph node or lung. One attractive option for such cases is immunotherapy. We propose using mechanical high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) to kill tumor cells and release antigens from tumors, stimulating the patients anti-tumor immune response. We hope to find out if HIFU application can both kill tumor cells and activate the immune system in cats. To determine if the treatment is effective, we are recruiting cats with soft tissue sarcomas located in the skin to undergo HIFU treatment prior to surgical removal of the tumor. Study Design Prior to enrolling in the study, your cat must undergo cancer staging, including a complete physical exam, lab work, tumor biopsy and a CT scan. These procedures are at owner expense. Your cats fur/hair will be clipped over the tumor as is standard for any ultrasound in cats. The treatment will be delivered in a series of bursts of sound that will be focused on the tumor to kill the cancerous cells through unbroken skin surface. The HIFU treatment is expected to take 30-60 minutes, but may take longer for some patients. Your cat may be sent home the same day, or if due to timing of the treatment or for the safety of your pet, s/he may need to stay overnight while recovering from anesthesia. Your cat's surgery will take place at the Veterinary Teaching Hospital in Blacksburg, VA 4-6 days following treatment. The goal of this study is to identify a maximally tolerated dose (MTD) of TdCyd and Aza-TdC in tumor-bearing dogs. A secondary goal is to evaluate the metabolism of the drugs as well as the effects on the tumor. Multiple companies are offering services that recommend \"targeted therapy\" for dogs with cancer, using drugs that are approved for the treatment of some types of cancer in humans. However, most of these drugs have not been studied for effectiveness in dogs, nor do we know how much or how often they should be given. The goal of this study is to measure levels over 24-96 hours of these drugs following a single oral or subcutaneous dose, in pet dogs with cancer. Dogs will receive a single oral or subcutaneous dose of a given agent at the dose recommended by the company, followed by blood collection 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 24 hours later. For one specific drug, samples will also be collected 0.25, 48, and 96 hours post-treatment. Following the 24- or 96-hour blood collection, dogs will be off study and eligible for any other treatment.

\n

Your dog will receive a single oral or subcutaneous dose of one of these drugs at a dose that is predicted to cause no side effects. A small amount of blood (approximately 1 teaspoon) will be collected at the time points above. Collection of the blood samples will take all day. Your dog will need to return the following day for 1 additional blood draw, or alternatively, they can stay overnight at no cost to you. Some dogs will need to return for blood collection 48 and 96 hours after administration. After the 24- or 96-hour blood sample is drawn, the study is over and your dog is eligible to receive any additional treatment that is recommended.

\n

Although the drugs we are studying have caused minimal side effects in laboratory dogs at the doses we are planning to use (even when given every day for several weeks), they have not been studied in pet dogs, which may be older and have other medical issues. Therefore, side effects (although extremely unlikely) could range from mild to severe, up to and including the death of your dog. Medications will be provided as needed to treat/prevent any side effects that might occur.

\n

Costs covered by the clinical trial for eligible enrolled dogs include the cost of all examinations, drug dispensing, and blood collection. You will be responsible for the initial exam fee, and tests to confirm that your dog is eligible. Participating owners will receive a $500 credit to their dog\u2019s Veterinary Teaching Hospital account, which can be applied to the initial testing or used to reduce costs of other cancer treatment when the study is complete.

regurgitation is a common side effect of general anesthesia in dogs and is of significant clinical concern due to the increased risk for aspiration pneumonia (lung infection due to inhaling stomach contents when regurgitation occurs). Dogs known to be at high risk for this include brachycephalic (dogs with short noses/flat faces) and dogs undergoing orthopedic or gastrointestinal surgery. A major contributing factor to postoperative regurgitation is the effect of the opioid pain medications that are administered as part of the patients analgesic plan. While opioids are the best method of pain control available, they can reduce peristalsis (the normal movement of the intestines), leading to undesired side effects such as regurgitation and constipation. The current gold standard to prevent postoperative vomiting is to administer an antinausea drug called maropitant citrate prior to surgery. Maropitant works within the portion of the brain that controls nausea in order to prevent vomiting; however, it does not target the underlying factors contributing to the postoperative regurgitation (reduced peristalsis) and will therefore not have an effect on reducing regurgitation or constipation.Methylnaltrexone (MNTX) is an opioid blocker (i.e. inhibits the effects of opioids). MNTX is able to specifically inhibit the effect of opioids within the intestines (i.e. preventing the loss of peristalsis) while preserving the opioids pain reducing properties. This means your pet will still receive the beneficial pain control normally achieved through opioids, but will not be at as high of a risk for postoperative complications brought on by regurgitation. Osteosarcoma is the most common malignant bone tumor in the dog. While surgery and chemotherapy are the main treatments for most osteosarcomas, most dogs will unfortunately eventually develop spread of their tumor. New treatments are needed to improve the outcome in both canine and human patients with osteosarcoma. Vismodegib is a drug that is approved for the treatment of basal cell carcinoma, a type of skin cancer, in humans. It appears that canine and human osteosarcoma, like human basal cell carcinoma, rely on a cell signaling pathway called the Hedgehog pathway (which is inhibited by vismodegib) for cell growth, survival and spread, and in mouse models of osteosarcoma, treatment with vismodegib results in delayed osteosarcoma spread, Vismodegib has been studied in laboratory dogs for safety, but has not been studied for the treatment of canine cancer. The primary objective of this study is to evaluate the safety and molecular effects of vismodegib treatment, combined with surgery and chemotherapy, in dogs with osteosarcoma. After amputation, your dog will receive vismodegib orally once daily, and will receive a total of 4 doses of carboplatin as an injection every 3 weeks for 4 treatments. They will be rechecked 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 11, 14 and 17 weeks after treatment is started and monthly thereafter, with every-other-month rechecks of chest X-rays. Visits will generally take about 4 hours. They will be eligible to continue receiving treatment as long as the drugs are tolerated and your dog is experiencing clinical benefit (no evidence of tumor spread). Analysis for tumor spread will be performed by monthly physical examinations and every-other-month chest X-rays. Standard bloodwork and urinalysis will be performed at each visit. Small skin biopsies (around the size of a pencil eraser) will be performed at the time of amputation and 2 and 8 weeks after starting vismodegib. Additional tests to be performed include periodic extra blood draws to look at the effect of vismodegib on cell function. The total volume of blood involved in each collection is approximately 5 teaspoons.

Osteosarcoma is a common cancer in dogs. Current treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy and various types of chemotherapy; however, there are few efficacious therapy options for dogs with osteosarcoma targeted to treat macroscopic OS metastases to the lungs. Recent studies show that certain immune cells, such as monocytes and regulatory T lymphocytes, play an important role in tumor metastasis in osteosarcoma and other cancer types. Certain anti-tumor drugs, like toceranib (PalladiaTM), have been show to suppress these cells and help the immune system better recognize cancer. Toceranib is an oral drug that inhibits the function of a group of proteins (receptor tyrosine kinases) important for cancer growth. Toceranib is approved by the FDA for the treatment of canine mast cell tumors, but there is preliminary evidence that some dogs with osteosarcoma may benefit from toceranib therapy. In recent studies, we have determined that treatment with the combination of high-dose losartan and toceranib can significantly slow tumor growth and, in some cases, stimulate significant tumor shrinkage in dogs with macroscopic OS lung metastases. More recent studies indicate that the use of a drug called defactinib may complement the activities of toceranib and losartan. The purpose of this trial is to determine whether the 3-drug combination of Palladia, losartan, and defactinib can give better cancer control in dogs with metastatic OS than the original 2-drug combination (Palladia/losartan). A secondary goal of this study is to assess gene expression in a type of immune cell called macrophages present in the lungs of dogs with metastatic OS. This will be accomplished through a procedure called bronchoalveolar lavage. Initially, your pet will undergo a series of diagnostic tests which may include blood tests, urinalyses, blood pressure, and x-rays of the chest. Test results will help determine if your pet is eligible to enter this clinical trial. These tests are routinely performed in patients with osteosarcoma and may be done even if you decide that your pet will not participate in a clinical trial. Following enrollment into the trial, your dog will undergo pre-treatment bronchoalveolar lavage under general anesthesia. This must be done prior to Day 0, but cannot be scheduled on the same day. Day 0 will be scheduled one to two days following bronchoalveolar lavage and involves the first administration of study drugs, then serial blood sample collection over 8 hours. We will collect more study blood the following day, 24 hrs after the first doses of medications. You will be sent home with oral losartan (twice daily) and oral defactinib (once daily), and oral toceranib (once every other day) after the 24 hour blood sample is collected. Your dog will then return two weeks later (Week 2) for study blood collection. At Week 4, your dog will return for chest x-rays, blood pressure, blood and urine tests and study blood collection. One month later (Week 8), your dog will return for the second broncheoalveolar lavage performed under general anesthesia, chest x-rays, blood and urine tests, and blood collection for study purposes. Follow-up visits will be required 4 weeks thereafter until disease progression is identified. Blood will be collected for study purposes (~1.5 tablespoons) at every visit for the study. Chest x-rays will be performed prior to enrollment and monthly thereafter. Blood pressure will be performed on Day 0, Week 4, Week 12, and monthly thereafter. Dogs will remain on the study as long as their pulmonary nodules do not progress in size and no new nodules are identified on chest x-rays. If your dog dies while on the study, a post-mortem examination and tumor collection may be necessary to explain the cause of death. This study is not randomized and there is no placebo group all dogs will receive all study treatments.

Lymphoma comprises approximately 25% of all canine cancers. Up to 40% of these cases are caused by T lymphocytes, known as peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL). The vast majority of lymphoma cases cannot be addressed with surgery and instead warrant chemotherapy. The standard of care chemotherapy protocol for lymphoma is abbreviated CHOP, which stands for the 4 drugs involved. Generally, dogs with PTCL treated with CHOP chemotherapy tend to experience shorter remission durations and overall survival than dogs with diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL). When treated with CHOP chemotherapy, PTCL dogs have a median survival time of 4-9 months while DLBCL dogs have a median survival time of 11-13 months. Previous studies have questioned whether other, non-CHOP protocols may be better suited for dogs with PTCL in hopes of increasing remission and survival times. One protocol that has been repeatedly investigated is LOPP chemotherapy. This protocol uses two of the same drugs as CHOP and two that are different. Recent studies have demonstrated with dogs with PTCL treated with LOPP can experience survival times closer to 11-17 months. While these findings are promising, none of these investigations have had a control arm of dogs receiving CHOP chemotherapy. The purpose of this study is to provide a direct comparison between the outcomes for dogs with peripheral T cell lymphoma (PTCL) treated with CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. The findings of this study could help veterinarians understand if one protocol is truly superior to the other for dogs with PTCL. In this study, your dog will be randomly selected to receive either CHOP or LOPP chemotherapy. At each visit, their lymph node size, blood work, and overall wellbeing will be assessed. Urothelial carcinoma (also known as transitional cell carcinoma) is the most common type of bladder cancer to affect dogs. Treatment often involves a combination of surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation therapy, with the aim being to reduce the size of the tumor, alleviate symptoms, and improve the dog's quality of life. In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a promising treatment approach for many types of cancer, including canine urothelial carcinoma. Immunotherapies aim to harness the body's immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. They can be particularly attractive for treating cancers that are difficult to access surgically or that have metastasized (spread to other parts of the body).This study seeks to evaluate a novel immunotherapy when used in dogs with urothelial carcinoma. The therapy specifically targets an important molecule primarily expressed on immune cells, which usually turns off the immune cells and prevents overactive immune responses. However, it also turns off anti-cancer immune responses and prevents the immune system controlling and killing cancer cells. Immunotherapies that are able to inhibit this molecule on immune cells that recognize cancer cells could make it possible for the immune system to recognize and attack the underlying cancer more effectively.Urothelial carcinoma in dogs shares many biological and molecular features with human urothelial carcinoma, including their ability to be shielded from the immune system. Human clinical trials in urothelial carcinoma investigating similar immunotherapies have shown these therapies to be more effective than traditional chemotherapies in some cases. Development of an immunotherapy that is safe and beneficial in canine urothelial carcinoma patients will advance veterinarians ability to treat this disease and will provide an important model to inform future canine and human clinical trials in this area. This study seeks to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of this novel immunotherapy in dogs with urothelial carcinoma.

Sinonasal cancer is smaller subgroup of head and neck cancers; however, sinonasal carcinoma is an important cancer globally, as it has the second highest occupational attributable fraction of all types of cancer. Despite improvements in the fields of surgery and radiation therapy, the prognosis remains poor for human patients diagnosed with this tumor type as most succumb to local tumor recurrence. Using the dog as a model for the human disease may help speed progress in developing new approaches to treatment of this cancer. Sinonasal carcinoma occurs commonly in dogs and is primarily treated with radiation therapy. Like humans, most dogs succumb to local tumor recurrence. With these clinical similarities, dogs could fill an unmet need for an effective model for human sinonasal carcinoma. In this study, we aim to evaluate a new radiation treatment known as Lattice Radiation Therapy (LRT). A current method of radiation therapy used to treat canine sinonasal carcinoma (SC), called stereotactic body radiotherapy therapy (SBRT), distributes a high dose of radiation uniformly across the tumor. Lattice radiation therapy (LRT) differs from SBRT in that instead of administering that uniform high dose of radiation throughout the tumor, several small spheres of high dose radiation are administered within the tumor and the rest of the tumor receives a lower dose of radiation. LRT has shown promise in early studies to provide tumor control with low normal tissue toxicity, suspected to be due to improved blood flow and immune responses compared to uniform, high dose radiation therapy. Our goal is to look at the differences in the tumors immune response during and after treatment as well as the clinical response with LRT compared to our standard SBRT. Dogs enrolled into this study will be treated with LRT. Prior to starting treatment, all dogs will have a CT scan and a nasal flush under anesthesia. The following procedures will be performed in all dogs enrolled in the study: CT scan for radiation therapy planning Lattice radiation therapy; 3 treatments given once daily over consecutive business days under general anesthesia Nasal flush, 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Blood collection (9-19 mL), 5 time points: prior to LRT, following 3rd fraction of LRT, 2 weeks following LRT, 3 months following LRT, and 6 months following LRT Tumor biopsy at the 2 week post-LRT time point under general anesthesia Recheck CT scan 3, 6, 12 months, and 18-months post-LRT under general anesthesia.

Hemangiosarcoma (HSA) is a highly aggressive and malignant vascular tumor occurring most commonly in dogs. Dogs with splenic hemangiosarcoma have a poor prognosis, with fewer than 20% of dogs surviving 9 months with surgery and adjuvant doxorubicin chemotherapy. Paclitaxel is one of the most effective anticancer agents used in human cancer today, with potent activity against a wide variety of tumors. Paclitaxel interferes with normal microtubule function during cell division and induces cell cycle arrest. In addition, several studies have shown that paclitaxel has antiangiogenic properties. Paclitaxel targets both the tumor stroma and the vasculature, and it has been shown to inducetumor control in human patients with soft tissue angiosarcomas. The conventional formulation of paclitaxel (Taxol) has been associated with acute adverse events in dogs, which has largely precluded the use of paclitaxel as a chemotherapeutic in veterinary oncology. The investigational drug to be used in this study, Paccal Vet, uses a proprietary formulation based on retinol derivatives (XR-17), which encapsulate paclitaxel to form nanosized micelles. Previous studies with Paccal Vet have demonstrated a tolerability profile that is generally similar to other chemotherapy drugs used in veterinary oncology. Moreover, anti-tumor activity in selected cancers in dogs, including mast cell tumors, squamous cell carcinoma, and mammary cancer has also been reported for Paccal Vet. These findings suggest that Paccal Vet may be a promising treatment option for dogs with hemangiosarcoma. It is important to note that none of the chemotherapeutic agents commonly used in veterinary oncology clinics for the treatment of hemangiosarcoma have been approved for veterinary use.
